questions.question: What does WORM stand for in the context of S3 Object Lock?

options.text: Write Once, Read Many
Write Once, Remove Manually
Write Only, Read Many
Write Once, Retain Memory

explanation.correct: WORM stands for Write Once, Read Many — once an object is uploaded and locked, it can be read many times but cannot be modified or deleted.
explanation.why: B, C, and D are incorrect. The concept is about allowing unlimited reads while preventing any writes (including deletes) after the initial upload.

questions.question: Which of the following is a MANDATORY prerequisite for enabling S3 Object Lock?

options.text: Block Public Access must be enabled
Versioning must be enabled on the bucket
Default encryption must be set to SSE-KMS
The bucket must be in a single AWS region

explanation.correct: S3 Object Lock requires versioning to be enabled on the bucket. Without versioning, you cannot enable Object Lock.
explanation.why: Block Public Access, SSE-KMS, and region restrictions are not prerequisites for Object Lock.

questions.question: What is the default encryption method applied automatically to all new S3 objects?

options.text: SSE-KMS with AWS Managed Keys
Client-Side Encryption
SSE-S3 (AES-256, S3 Managed Keys)
SSE-C (Customer Provided Keys)

explanation.correct: SSE-S3 is the default encryption — Amazon S3 automatically encrypts every new object using AES-256 with keys that S3 manages entirely. No configuration is required.
explanation.why: SSE-KMS requires explicit configuration. Client-side encryption is done by the user. SSE-C requires the customer to provide keys per request.

questions.question: What does DEK stand for in the context of AWS KMS and S3 encryption?

options.text: Domain Encryption Key
Data Encryption Key
Derived Encryption Keystore
Default Encryption Key

explanation.correct: DEK stands for Data Encryption Key — a temporary key generated by KMS that is used by S3 to actually encrypt the object data.
explanation.why: Domain Encryption Key, Derived Encryption Keystore, and Default Encryption Key are not AWS terms.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of enabling S3 Bucket Key for SSE-KMS encrypted buckets?

options.text: Increases the strength of encryption from AES-128 to AES-256
Reduces the number of KMS API calls, lowering KMS costs by up to 99%
Enables automatic key rotation every 90 days
Allows objects to be decrypted without an IAM role

explanation.correct: S3 Bucket Key reduces KMS API calls by generating a long-lived bucket-level DEK that is reused for many objects, instead of calling KMS for every individual object. This can reduce KMS costs by up to 99%.
explanation.why: Bucket Key does not change encryption strength, enable key rotation, or bypass IAM requirements.

questions.question: In Object Lock Compliance Mode, who can delete or modify a locked object during its retention period?

options.text: Only the AWS root user
Only IAM users with the s3:DeleteObject permission
AWS Support with a valid support case
Nobody — not even AWS or the root user

explanation.correct: In Compliance Mode, absolutely nobody can delete or modify the object during the retention period — not authorised users, not the root user, and not AWS itself. This is the strictest protection level.
explanation.why: Governance Mode allows root/authorised users to overwrite (though not delete). Compliance Mode is absolute — no exceptions.

questions.question: What is the key difference between Object Lock Governance Mode and Compliance Mode?

options.text: Governance Mode protects from deletion only; Compliance Mode also prevents reads
Governance Mode allows authorised users to overwrite objects; Compliance Mode allows no modifications by anyone
Governance Mode requires KMS encryption; Compliance Mode works with SSE-S3
Governance Mode is for individual objects; Compliance Mode applies to entire buckets

explanation.correct: Governance Mode protects from deletion but allows authorised users (with special IAM permissions like root) to overwrite/modify the object. Compliance Mode prevents all modifications and deletions by everyone, including AWS.
explanation.why: Neither mode prevents reads. Neither requires specific encryption. Both can be applied at object or bucket level.

questions.question: Which S3 encryption option is being blocked for all NEW S3 buckets from April 2026?

options.text: SSE-S3
SSE-KMS
SSE-C (Customer Provided Keys)
Client-Side Encryption

explanation.correct: SSE-C (Customer Provided Keys) is being blocked for new S3 buckets from April 2026 due to AWS security concerns about customers managing and transmitting their own keys over the API.
explanation.why: SSE-S3 is the default and remains available. SSE-KMS is the recommended production choice. Client-Side Encryption is managed entirely by the customer outside of S3.

questions.question: What is Cross-Region Replication (CRR) primarily used for?

options.text: Automatically deleting old objects in a different region
Copying objects to a bucket in a different AWS region for DR, compliance, or latency
Synchronising object ACLs across all regions automatically
Replicating encryption keys to another KMS region

explanation.correct: CRR automatically copies objects from a source bucket to a destination bucket in a different AWS region. This is used for disaster recovery, regulatory compliance requiring geographic distribution, and reducing latency for users in other regions.
explanation.why: CRR does not handle deletion automation (that is lifecycle rules), sync ACLs automatically, or replicate KMS keys.

questions.question: Which of the following must be enabled on BOTH the source and destination buckets for replication to work?

options.text: Object Lock
Static Website Hosting
Versioning
Default Encryption

explanation.correct: Versioning must be enabled on both the source and destination buckets before S3 replication can be configured. This is a mandatory prerequisite.
explanation.why: Object Lock, Static Website Hosting, and Default Encryption are not required for replication, though encryption can be configured as an option.

questions.question: A lifecycle rule is configured to transition objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 90 days. An object was uploaded 60 days before the lifecycle rule was created. When will this object transition?

options.text: 30 days after the rule was created (because 60 days have already passed)
The object will never be transitioned because it predates the rule
90 days from today, regardless of when the object was uploaded
90 days from when the object was originally uploaded — which is 30 days from now

explanation.correct: Lifecycle rules evaluate object age from the date the object was originally uploaded, not from when the rule was created. If the object is already 60 days old and the rule triggers at 90 days, the transition will happen 30 days from now (when the object turns 90 days old).
explanation.why: Lifecycle rules do apply to existing objects as long as they match the rule's scope. The clock starts from the object's creation/upload date.

questions.question: What does S3 Replication Time Control (RTC) guarantee?

options.text: Objects are replicated within 1 second
99.99% of objects are replicated within 15 minutes with CloudWatch monitoring
Objects are replicated synchronously before the upload acknowledgement is returned
Objects are replicated to all AWS regions simultaneously

explanation.correct: S3 Replication Time Control (RTC) provides an SLA guaranteeing that 99.99% of objects will be replicated within 15 minutes, with real-time monitoring available via CloudWatch metrics.
explanation.why: Standard replication is asynchronous with no SLA. RTC does not provide sub-second or synchronous replication, nor does it replicate to all regions.

questions.question: You enable CRR on a production S3 bucket. You notice that 500,000 existing objects in the bucket are NOT present in the destination bucket. How do you replicate those existing objects?

options.text: Disable and re-enable the replication rule
Manually copy each object using the AWS CLI cp command
Use S3 Batch Replication to backfill existing objects
Existing objects are automatically replicated within 24 hours

explanation.correct: S3 Replication only applies to new objects uploaded after the rule is created. To replicate existing objects, you must use S3 Batch Replication — a separate operation specifically designed to backfill existing objects into the destination bucket.
explanation.why: Disabling/re-enabling rules does not trigger replication of existing objects. Manual CLI copy is impractical at scale. Existing objects are NOT automatically replicated.

questions.question: Why does S3 use a DEK (Data Encryption Key) instead of directly using the KMS master key to encrypt object data?

options.text: DEKs are stronger than KMS master keys
KMS master keys are stored in HSMs and cannot be extracted — S3 generates a DEK from the master key to perform actual encryption without exposing the master key
Using DEKs avoids the need to pay for KMS API calls
DEKs are automatically rotated every 24 hours for better security

explanation.correct: KMS master keys are stored in tamper-proof Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) and can never be extracted. S3 cannot directly use the master key on data. Instead, KMS generates a DEK derived from the master key, which S3 uses for actual encryption. The master key's security is preserved inside the HSM.
explanation.why: DEKs are not inherently stronger. Using DEKs does not eliminate KMS API calls (those are reduced by Bucket Key). DEK rotation is not automatic at 24-hour intervals.

questions.question: What is the minimum number of days an object must remain in S3 Standard before a lifecycle rule can transition it to S3 Standard-IA?

options.text: 1 day
14 days
30 days
90 days

explanation.correct: Objects must remain in S3 Standard for at least 30 days before they can be transitioned to S3 Standard-IA or One Zone-IA via lifecycle rules. This is an AWS minimum enforced constraint.
explanation.why: 1 day and 14 days are less than the minimum. 90 days is excessive for this specific transition — that threshold applies to other rules but not the S3 Standard → Standard-IA transition.

questions.question: For static website hosting on S3, which of the following accurately describes the HTTPS limitation?

options.text: S3 static website hosting supports HTTPS natively if you enable it in bucket settings
HTTPS is only available for buckets in the US East (N. Virginia) region
S3 static website hosting only supports HTTP; CloudFront with ACM is needed for HTTPS
HTTPS requires enabling SSE-KMS encryption on the bucket

explanation.correct: S3 static website hosting natively serves content over HTTP only. To serve over HTTPS with a custom domain, you must put a CloudFront distribution in front of the S3 bucket and attach an ACM (AWS Certificate Manager) SSL/TLS certificate to CloudFront.
explanation.why: There is no HTTPS toggle in S3 website hosting. The limitation is not region-specific. SSE-KMS encryption is about data at rest, not in-transit HTTPS.

questions.question: Which S3 lifecycle action permanently deletes objects after a specified number of days?

options.text: Transition action
Expiration action
Archival action
Purge action

explanation.correct: Expiration actions in S3 lifecycle rules permanently delete objects (or delete specific object versions if versioning is enabled) after a specified number of days from the object's creation date.
explanation.why: Transition actions move objects to a different storage class. Archival action and Purge action are not valid S3 lifecycle action types.

questions.question: In SSE-KMS, what exactly encrypts the actual S3 object data?

options.text: The KMS master key directly
The HSM hardware module
The Data Encryption Key (DEK)
The S3 service using AES-256 without involving KMS

explanation.correct: In SSE-KMS, the DEK (Data Encryption Key) is what actually encrypts the S3 object data. The KMS master key is used to generate and wrap the DEK, but the DEK performs the actual object-level encryption. The encrypted DEK is then stored alongside the encrypted object.
explanation.why: The KMS master key never leaves the HSM — it cannot directly encrypt data files. The HSM is hardware storage, not an encryption actor on objects. SSE-KMS specifically involves KMS.

questions.question: What is the difference between Same-Region Replication (SRR) and Cross-Region Replication (CRR)?

options.text: SRR is free; CRR incurs data transfer charges
SRR copies to a bucket in the same region; CRR copies to a bucket in a different AWS region
SRR requires versioning; CRR does not
SRR supports KMS encryption; CRR does not support encrypted objects

explanation.correct: SRR (Same-Region Replication) copies objects to a destination bucket within the same AWS region, while CRR (Cross-Region Replication) copies objects to a destination bucket in a different AWS region.
explanation.why: Both SRR and CRR require versioning. Both support encrypted objects. While CRR does incur inter-region data transfer charges, SRR may still have intra-region costs — the fundamental difference is geographic scope.

questions.question: A company needs to retain regulatory data in S3 for exactly 7 years and prevent any deletion even by accidental admin actions. Which Object Lock configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Governance Mode with a 7-year retention period
Legal Hold with no expiry
Compliance Mode with a 7-year retention period
SSE-KMS with key rotation disabled for 7 years

explanation.correct: Compliance Mode with a 7-year retention period ensures that absolutely no one — including root users and AWS — can delete or modify the objects for exactly 7 years. This satisfies strict regulatory retention requirements with a defined end date.
explanation.why: Governance Mode allows authorised users to overwrite objects, which does not meet the 'no deletion even by admins' requirement. Legal Hold has no defined end date. SSE-KMS controls encryption, not deletion protection.

questions.question: You are designing a multi-account AWS environment where Account A (production) replicates S3 objects to Account B (disaster recovery). What configuration is required on the Account B destination bucket?

options.text: Account B must have the same IAM roles as Account A
Account B destination bucket policy must explicitly grant Account A permission to replicate objects into it
Account B must be in a different region than Account A for cross-account replication to work
Account B must subscribe to S3 Replication in AWS Marketplace

explanation.correct: For cross-account replication, the destination bucket in Account B must have a bucket policy that explicitly grants Account A's replication IAM role permission to write (replicate) objects into the destination bucket. Without this, the replication will fail with access denied errors.
explanation.why: IAM roles do not transfer between accounts. Cross-account replication does not require different regions (you can also do same-region cross-account replication). There is no S3 Marketplace subscription.

questions.question: Your S3 bucket has a lifecycle rule transitioning all objects to Glacier Deep Archive after 180 days. An auditor requires you to retrieve a specific file from 2 years ago within 12 hours. What is the restoration path?

options.text: The file is permanently deleted after 180 days in Glacier Deep Archive
Request a Glacier Deep Archive retrieval; Standard retrieval takes 12 hours, Bulk takes up to 48 hours
Disable the lifecycle rule to restore the object automatically
Move the file from Glacier Deep Archive to Standard using S3 Batch Operations instantly

explanation.correct: Objects in Glacier Deep Archive are not deleted — they are archived. To access them, you initiate a restore request. Standard retrieval from Glacier Deep Archive takes up to 12 hours. Bulk retrieval is cheaper but can take up to 48 hours. After restoration, a temporary copy is available in S3 for the period you specify.
explanation.why: Lifecycle rules transition objects, not delete them (unless you add an expiration rule). Disabling the lifecycle rule does not automatically restore objects. There is no instant restore from Glacier Deep Archive — it always takes hours.

questions.question: A KMS Customer Managed Key has key rotation enabled. An object was encrypted with an older version of the key before rotation. What happens when you try to decrypt the object after the key has been rotated?

options.text: Decryption fails because the old key version is deleted during rotation
You must manually re-encrypt the object with the new key version
KMS automatically retains all previous key versions and uses the correct version to decrypt the object
You must disable key rotation to decrypt objects encrypted with older key versions

explanation.correct: When KMS rotates a key, it creates a new key version but retains all previous versions. KMS automatically tracks which key version was used to encrypt each object and uses the correct (older) version to decrypt it. You do not need to re-encrypt existing objects after rotation.
explanation.why: Old key material is never deleted during rotation — that would make existing encrypted data unrecoverable. Re-encryption is optional, not required. Disabling rotation is unnecessary for decryption.

questions.question: Your organisation uses S3 static website hosting with a custom domain (www.mycompany.com). Users report the site loads slowly in Europe. Which combination of services resolves this while maintaining HTTPS?

options.text: S3 Transfer Acceleration + Route53
CloudFront (CDN) + ACM (SSL certificate) + Route53 (DNS)
S3 Replication to a European region + static website hosting enabled in that region
Increase S3 storage class to S3 Standard with no other changes

explanation.correct: CloudFront is a Content Delivery Network that caches your S3 static website content at edge locations worldwide (including Europe), dramatically reducing latency for international users. ACM provides a free SSL certificate attached to CloudFront for HTTPS. Route53 resolves your custom domain to the CloudFront distribution. This is the standard production architecture.
explanation.why: S3 Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads to S3, not downloads to end users. Replication creates another origin but does not provide CDN edge caching or HTTPS. Storage class changes do not affect delivery speed.

questions.question: A lifecycle rule is configured with a transition to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days and Glacier after 90 days. Versioning is enabled. A developer deletes an object on Day 45, creating a delete marker. What happens to the non-current version?

options.text: The non-current version is immediately deleted along with the delete marker
The non-current version continues its lifecycle independently — it can be configured with separate non-current version transition/expiration rules
The non-current version is permanently locked and can never be transitioned
The lifecycle rule stops applying to that object once a delete marker is created

explanation.correct: When versioning is enabled and an object is deleted (creating a delete marker), the previous version becomes a non-current version. Lifecycle rules support separate actions for non-current versions — you can configure them to transition to cheaper storage or expire independently of current version rules.
explanation.why: Non-current versions are not immediately deleted. Lifecycle rules apply independently to current and non-current versions. Delete markers do not stop lifecycle evaluation.

questions.question: You have a bucket policy that denies any s3:PutObject request unless the upload includes a specific KMS key ARN in the format arn:aws:kms:region:account-id:key/key-id. A developer uploads a file without specifying any encryption key. What happens?

options.text: The upload succeeds and is encrypted with SSE-S3 by default
The upload succeeds but remains unencrypted
The upload is denied by the bucket policy condition
The upload succeeds but the object is immediately deleted by the policy

explanation.correct: The bucket policy has an explicit Deny condition that rejects uploads not using the specified KMS key ARN. Since the developer did not include the KMS key in the upload request, the condition is triggered and the upload is denied with an Access Denied error. The policy overrides the default SSE-S3 encryption behaviour.
explanation.why: Bucket policy Deny conditions are evaluated before default encryption settings. The upload cannot succeed or be silently re-encrypted — a Deny is a hard block.

questions.question: What is the format of a KMS Key ARN used when specifying an encryption key for S3 object uploads?

options.text: kms://region/account-id/key-id
arn:aws:kms:region:account-id:key/key-id
aws:kms:key:region:key-id
s3://kms/region/key-id

explanation.correct: The correct KMS Key ARN format is arn:aws:kms:region:account-id:key/key-id — for example, arn:aws:kms:ap-south-1:123456789012:key/abc123-def4-5678-gh90-ijklmno12345. This ARN format is required when specifying a KMS key in S3 upload properties or bucket policies.
explanation.why: The other formats are all invented and not valid AWS ARN formats.

questions.question: S3 static website hosting serves content over HTTP. What is the standard production architecture to serve a static website over HTTPS with a custom domain and low global latency?

options.text: S3 + Load Balancer + SSL certificate installed on Load Balancer
S3 + EC2 reverse proxy with Nginx + ACM
S3 (origin) + CloudFront (CDN + HTTPS) + ACM (certificate) + Route53 (DNS)
S3 + API Gateway + Lambda for HTTPS termination

explanation.correct: The standard serverless architecture is S3 as the origin (storing the static files), CloudFront as the CDN (providing edge caching worldwide and HTTPS via ACM certificate), ACM (AWS Certificate Manager providing free SSL/TLS certificate), and Route53 (DNS to map custom domain to CloudFront). This is scalable, serverless, and cost-effective.
explanation.why: Load Balancers and EC2 are server-based approaches — not serverless and more expensive. API Gateway + Lambda is for APIs, not static file serving.

questions.question: Which Object Lock feature has NO defined expiry date and keeps an object locked indefinitely until explicitly removed?

options.text: Retention Period
Legal Hold
Governance Mode
Compliance Mode

explanation.correct: Legal Hold has no expiry date — the object remains locked until an authorised user explicitly removes the legal hold. This is distinct from Retention Period which has a specific end date. Legal Hold is typically used during active litigation where the duration cannot be predicted in advance.
explanation.why: Retention Period has a defined end date. Governance Mode and Compliance Mode are retention enforcement modes — they work in combination with either Retention Period or Legal Hold.

questions.question: Your company processes 1 million new S3 objects daily, all encrypted with SSE-KMS using a Customer Managed Key. You notice the monthly KMS bill is unexpectedly high. What is the most cost-effective solution that maintains the same security level?

options.text: Switch to SSE-S3 encryption to eliminate KMS charges
Enable S3 Bucket Key on the bucket to reuse a single bucket-level DEK and reduce KMS API calls by up to 99%
Reduce the number of objects uploaded per day
Switch to client-side encryption to bypass KMS charges

explanation.correct: S3 Bucket Key reduces KMS API calls dramatically by generating a single long-lived bucket-level DEK from one KMS call, and reusing it for all objects in the bucket. This maintains the same SSE-KMS security model (same key policies, same audit trail) while reducing KMS API call charges by up to 99%.
explanation.why: Switching to SSE-S3 removes the KMS audit trail and key control — not acceptable for regulated environments. Reducing upload volume is a business constraint, not a cost-optimisation solution. Client-side encryption shifts key management complexity to you.
